title: Change the Vendor's Bank Details Safely
skill: Master-data change control and fraud prevention
scenario: An email arrives: Northwind Fasteners (V-1042) says their bank account changed, please pay the next run to the new account. This is the single most common way companies lose money to fraud - a spoofed vendor email redirecting payment. You own the vendor master. Build the change-control record that verifies the request before one dollar moves.
inputLabel: The change request + the control you must apply
input:
Inbound request: an email, signed 'Northwind Accounts', asking to replace ACH ...4021 with a new account before today's 3:00 PM run. It includes a phone number to 'call with any questions'.

The control the desk requires for any bank-detail change:
- Verify by CALLING BACK on the number already ON FILE in the vendor master - never the number in the request. A spoofed email supplies a spoofed phone number.
- A second approver (the AP Manager) must sign off; the Vendor Relations Desk alone cannot change banking.
- Payments to this vendor are HELD until verification completes.
- The record's status stays 'pending-verification' until the callback confirms; only then is the change applied.

Build the vendor-change-control record that encodes exactly this.
instructions: Set changeType to bank-detail and vendorId to the vendor in the request (V-1042).
Record requestChannel as how it arrived (email) - the channel is itself a risk signal.
Set verificationMethod to callback and verificationContact to the number ON FILE, not the one in the email.
Set secondApprover to the AP Manager and paymentsHeld to true.
Set status to pending-verification (not applied) and validate.
copilotPrompt: Build a vendor bank-detail change-control record for V-1042 from an emailed request. Verification must be a callback to the number on file (not the email's number), the AP Manager is the second approver, payments are held, and status is pending-verification. Return JSON with changeType, vendorId, requestChannel, verificationMethod, verificationContact, secondApprover, paymentsHeld, status.
successMessage: Change queued, not applied. The callback to the on-file number - not the email's number - is the control that stops payment redirection fraud.

intro.heading: Before you touch the master: banking changes are a fraud target

sections.title: The master record is a payment instruction
sections.body: The vendor master says where money goes. Change one bank field and every future run pays the new account. That is why an emailed 'please update our bank details' is the classic business-email-compromise attack: change the record and the payment follows.

sections.title: Verify out of band, on the number you already trust
sections.body: The one control that defeats the attack: confirm the change by calling the number ALREADY ON FILE, not any contact the request supplied. A spoofed email carries a spoofed phone number that reaches the fraudster. Trusting the request to verify the request is the whole vulnerability.

sections.title: Dual control and a hold, not a quick edit
sections.body: One person editing banking on their own is how a single compromised login drains an account. A second approver and a payment hold turn the change into a reviewed event: nothing pays until the callback confirms and the AP Manager signs.

sections.title: Pending is a safe state
sections.body: The record does not apply the change; it records the change as pending-verification. An unverified banking change sitting in 'pending' costs nothing. An unverified change applied costs the whole run. Status is the difference.

takeaway.heading: The change is verified, not just accepted
points: You treated a bank-detail change as what it is - a payment instruction - and refused to apply it on the strength of the email that requested it.
The decisive control is the callback to the number on file: verifying a request with contact info the request supplied is the exact hole fraud walks through.
Dual control and a payment hold turned a one-click edit into a reviewed event, so no single compromised account can redirect a run.
Pending-verification is a safe, cheap state; the cost only appears if an unverified change is applied, and you did not apply it.
The workflow can now change high-risk master data through a verified, dual-controlled process instead of a trusting edit.
